report.source_text: Over the next 6 months, she presented to the ED three times with similar reports while intermittently being seen by multiple specialists as an outpatient. In rheumatology, autoimmune diseases including myositis were ruled out. Dermatology assessed large ‘birthmarks’ on her left leg (figure 3) and referred her to interventional radiology for suspected vascular malformations. The venogram performed by interventional radiology revealed arteriovenous fistulas in the left thigh (figure 4).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 20-year-old woman presented with acute worsening of chronic left thigh swelling and pain, a condition present since childhood with associated capillary malformations. Initial workup in the ED ruled out DVT (E002), fracture (E003), compartment syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis, and cellulitis (E006). Labs showed elevated d-dimer and creatine kinase (E001). MRI showed soft tissue edema but no arteriovenous (AV) malformation (E004). Rhabdomyolysis was considered the most likely diagnosis (E006), and the patient was treated and discharged after improvement (E007, E008). Over the next 6 months, she experienced recurrent symptoms. Rheumatology ruled out autoimmune diseases. Dermatology assessed her 'birthmarks' and referred her for suspected vascular malformations. An interventional radiology venogram subsequently revealed arteriovenous fistulas in the left thigh (E009). Finally, a genetic analysis revealing a RASA1 variant confirmed the diagnosis of Parkes-Weber syndrome (E009).

Interventional radiology venogram revealed arteriovenous fistulas in the left thigh.
Genetic analysis revealed a RASA1 variant (Chr5(GRCh37)g.86659154_86659158del).
